title: The Context of Our Character, Part 1
hook: The pledge on the wall works best before the raffle cash is counted.
counterintuition: Honesty feels like a trait you carry into the room, but the decisive moment is often the cue that appears before the excuse gets comfortable.
tryThisNow: Move one rule, pledge, or standard to the exact place where the questionable choice begins, before the private excuse starts.
keyTakeaway: Place honesty cues before the tempting choice, where they can interrupt rationalization early.

breakdown.fastRead:
Raffle stubs cover a folding table after the hall lights come up. The cash box is short, the count is messy, and a small rounding error would be easy to explain. Then the donor pledge is read aloud before counting begins.

Small dishonesty often survives by keeping a decent self-image intact. The cue has to arrive before the story of harmlessness is written.

Put the standard at the front of the act.
breakdown.deepRead:
In the matrix-task experiments, people cheated a little when they could gain and still feel honest. A timely moral reminder, such as recalling an honor code, reduced cheating even when enforcement did not change.

The cue did not turn bad people good. It changed the context before rationalization got started.

That timing is the lesson.

At a farmers market, Fiona sets an honor jar beside wrapped bouquets under a striped awning. Customers are not planning to steal. A few may shave a dollar because it feels neighborly and minor. Fiona moves a plain honesty note from behind the jar to eye level before the first customer takes flowers. The price did not change. The moment did.

The limit is that reminders are not a full ethics system. They work best on the gray edge, where people want to see themselves as honest and need the standard close enough to matter.

Julian uses the same timing in the archive. The handling oath had been kept on a wall sign, where patrons saw it after they had already chosen a folder. Moving the oath onto the box changes the first touch. The rule is no longer a reminder in the room; it is part of removing the folder.
breakdown.fullRead:
Most everyday dishonesty is not a grand declaration against honesty. It is a small adjustment wrapped in a story: everyone does it, it barely matters, I will fix it later, they will not miss it, the rule is fuzzy. The person keeps the mirror. The behavior bends.

At a fundraiser, Natalie is the volunteer treasurer. Raffle stubs are spread across a folding table, and the hall lights have just come up. Before counting cash, she reads the posted donor pledge aloud and initials the count sheet beside another volunteer. The second initials matter, but the first move matters more: the standard enters before the arithmetic gets convenient.

A moral reminder does its work by arriving early. After the questionable choice begins, the mind can become a lawyer for the choice it wants.

That is why the placement of a cue matters. A pledge buried in a handbook is weak. A fairness line at the top of a score form is stronger. A handling oath on top of a folder box is stronger than a rule posted behind the desk. The cue should sit where the hand is about to move.

Inside a local-history archive, cream-colored folders rest in a gray box beneath a cotton handling sheet. Julian worries patrons skip sign-out because the folder feels too minor to count as a loss. He places the handling oath on top of the folder box, so each patron touches it before removing a folder. The rule becomes part of the action, not a scolding afterward.

This is not about calling everyone dishonest. The design assumes something more generous and more useful: many people want to behave honestly, and context can either help that self win or give the excuse more room.

A youth soccer referee named Kate stands by a muddy fence with a damp score form. One team is local, and softening a yellow-card report would make the evening easier. Before filling in the card count, she reads the fairness line printed at the top. The line does not police her. It reminds her who she intends to be before the local pressure speaks.

Sylvia sees the same timing problem at a professional conference. When the attestation sits below the attendance checklist, people can claim credits and then treat the promise as a formality. Moving the attestation above the checklist makes the standard arrive before each box is checked. The form asks for honesty before convenience has written its excuse.

Punishment works on some problems. Surveillance works on some problems. This move is for the smaller, common place where the person still cares about being honest. Put the standard there, early, visible, and tied to the act.

An honesty cue that arrives after the excuse is late to the meeting.

examples.title: Natalie Reads the Donor Pledge Before Counting

planSpec.domain: charity raffle ticket counting after a fundraiser
planSpec.audience: a volunteer treasurer reconciling cash and unsold ticket stubs
planSpec.stakes: rounding in her own favor while still feeling like a good volunteer
planSpec.requiredBeat: before counting cash, the treasurer reads the posted donor pledge aloud and initials the count sheet beside another volunteer

examples.scenario: Raffle stubs spread across a folding table after the hall lights come up. Natalie is reconciling cash and unsold tickets, and a small rounding choice could favor her without looking like theft. Before she opens the cash box, she must decide whether to read the posted donor pledge aloud and initial the count sheet beside another volunteer. The pledge is not a speech; it is a speed bump before the arithmetic gets useful.
examples.whatToDo: Read the pledge before counting and require second initials on the count sheet. Put the donor standard in the room before the numbers get flexible.
examples.whyItMatters: The tempting lie is small enough to rationalize. An early pledge helps Natalie keep her honest self active before the rounding story begins.

examples.title: Fiona Moves the Honesty Note Above the Jar

planSpec.domain: farmers market honor jar for flower bouquets
planSpec.audience: a stall owner testing a payment setup when she steps away
planSpec.stakes: customers shaving a dollar while still seeing themselves as honest neighbors
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner moves a simple honesty note from behind the jar to eye level before the first customer takes a bouquet

examples.scenario: An honor jar sits beside wrapped flower bouquets under a striped awning. Fiona predicts customers will pay fairly, but she has seen a few short payments when the note sits behind the jar. Before the first customer takes a bouquet, she has to decide whether to move the honesty note to eye level and watch whether the bouquet price lands differently. The note is short enough to read while reaching, which is the only moment that matters.
examples.whatToDo: Move the honesty note where customers see it before touching the flowers. Let the standard meet the hand before the shortcut appears.
examples.whyItMatters: Shorting the jar can feel minor and neighborly. An eye-level cue makes the honest identity visible before the dollar gets shaved.

examples.title: Julian Places the Oath on the Folder Box

planSpec.domain: library self-checkout for rare local-history folders
planSpec.audience: an archivist worried about patrons skipping sign-out steps
planSpec.stakes: folders going missing because the act feels too minor to count as dishonesty
planSpec.requiredBeat: the archivist places the handling oath on top of the folder box, so patrons touch it before removing a folder

examples.scenario: Cream-colored archive folders sit in a gray box beneath a cotton handling sheet. Before patrons remove folders for self-checkout, Julian has to decide whether to place the handling oath on top of the box so each hand touches the promise first. The sign-out line is still simple. The difference is that the promise now sits under the hand before the folder leaves. Julian is not adding surveillance; he is moving the standard to the exact second when the shortcut begins.
examples.whatToDo: Place the handling oath on top of the box and keep the sign-out line beside it. Put the reminder in the path of the action.
examples.whyItMatters: Skipping sign-out feels small when the rule is distant. Touching the oath first makes the standard present before the folder is taken.

examples.title: Kate Reads the Fairness Line Before the Card Count

planSpec.domain: youth soccer referee assigning final score reports
planSpec.audience: a volunteer referee entering scores after a disputed match
planSpec.stakes: softening a yellow-card report because one team is local and the lie feels small
planSpec.requiredBeat: the referee reads the fairness line at the top of the score form before filling in the card count

examples.scenario: "They're our kids," the assistant coach says as rain drips from the fence. Kate has a damp score form clipped after a muddy match, and the local team is one card away from suspension trouble. Before filling the card count, she must decide whether to read the fairness line at the top of the form and enter what happened. The sentence at the top of the form gives her honest self the first word.
examples.whatToDo: Read the fairness line before writing the card count. Let the standard arrive before local loyalty softens the report.
examples.whyItMatters: The softened report would feel small and kind. The cue reminds Kate that accuracy is part of the role before the excuse can sound generous.

examples.title: Evan Taps the Member Agreement Before Minutes

planSpec.audience: a member logging laser-cutter minutes after a late session
planSpec.stakes: underreporting use because nobody was watching and the extra minutes feel harmless
planSpec.requiredBeat: after discrepancies appear, the shop moves the member agreement above the time keypad and asks members to tap it before entering minutes

examples.scenario: On Friday night at the makerspace, a laser-cutter keypad glows beside a stack of acrylic offcuts after a late session. Evan used extra minutes and almost rounds down. After discrepancies appear, the shop moves the member agreement above the time keypad and asks members to tap it before entering minutes. The log now starts with the promise, not the excuse. Evan now meets the shared-use rule before the flexible number field invites a story.
examples.whatToDo: Place the agreement above the keypad and require a tap before minute entry. Put the shared-use standard before the number.
examples.whyItMatters: Extra minutes feel harmless when nobody is watching. The agreement cue helps members report as the kind of people who keep the shop fair.

examples.title: Sylvia Moves the Attestation Above the Session Checklist

planSpec.audience: a conference organizer preventing inflated attendance claims
planSpec.stakes: attendees claiming credit for sessions they left early while preserving a professional self-image
planSpec.requiredBeat: after moving the professional attestation above the session checklist, claimed credits drop without extra policing

examples.scenario: Sylvia places a badge lanyard across a continuing-education checklist at the registration desk. She first finds inflated credits from attendees who left sessions early. After moving the professional attestation above the session checklist, claimed credits drop without extra policing. The same people now meet the standard before checking boxes, not after the convenient number is already chosen.
examples.whatToDo: Move the attestation above the checklist and require it before claimed credits. Put professional identity before the boxes.
examples.whyItMatters: Inflating credits can feel like paperwork, not dishonesty. The attestation makes the honest self salient before the check marks begin.

questions.prompt: A volunteer treasurer overstates a small reimbursement while still thinking of herself as honest and helpful. What mechanism best explains the risk?
choices: Small cheating can survive when it fits the person's self-concept.
Only dishonest people cheat in small ways.
Honesty cues work only when punishment increases.
questions.explanation: The issue is rationalized small cheating that preserves self-image. The scene does not require fixed bad character or higher punishment.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood flower stand uses an honor jar and finds people shorting payments by small amounts when the note sits behind the cash. Which change best applies the lesson?
choices: Move a simple honesty note to eye level before anyone takes the item.
Hide the price so people feel trusted.
Check the jar only at the end of the month.
questions.explanation: The early visible cue interrupts rationalization before the act. Hiding price or delaying checks gives the excuse more room.

questions.prompt: An archive loses folders because patrons skip a quick sign-out when the box feels informal and nobody is watching. Which design is strongest?
choices: Send a scolding email after each missing folder.
Place the handling oath on top of the folder box so patrons touch it before removal.
Make the sign-out sheet smaller so it feels less formal.
questions.explanation: The oath belongs before the choice, in the path of action. Scolding afterward is late, and a smaller sheet may make the rule easier to dismiss.

questions.prompt: A youth referee may soften a card report for the local team after a muddy match and a tense parent conversation. Which cue best protects the report?
choices: A fairness line read before entering the card count.
A reminder at the season-ending banquet.
A promise to try harder next match.
questions.explanation: The fairness line arrives at the decision point. Later reminders and vague promises do not interrupt the current rationalization.

questions.prompt: A makerspace moves its member agreement above the machine-time keypad after users round down late-session minutes. Why might this reduce underreporting?
choices: It makes users afraid of machine failure.
It reminds members of the shared-use standard before they enter a flexible number.
It turns tool use into a market norm.
questions.explanation: The agreement cue appears before the number can be rounded down. It activates identity and fairness, not fear of machines or pricing.

questions.prompt: A conference finds inflated attendance credits when attendees check boxes after leaving sessions early. Which placement of an attestation is most useful?
choices: After the checklist, so attendees can reflect once finished.
On the website weeks before registration only.
Above the session checklist, before attendees claim credits.
questions.explanation: The attestation should appear before the claims are made. Afterward or weeks earlier is weaker because the rationalization happens at the checklist.

questions.prompt: A manager says, 'We need cameras because reminders are naive,' after seeing small shortcuts in a checkout process. Which evaluation best fits this material?
choices: Reminders are useful mainly for gray-edge choices where people still want to see themselves as honest.
Reminders replace every enforcement system.
Cameras are always unethical.
questions.explanation: Moral reminders help when self-concept matters. They are not a full substitute for enforcement, and the point is not a blanket rejection of monitoring.

questions.prompt: A cashier signs an honesty pledge only after closing the till, and shortages continue during the count. What is likely wrong with the design?
choices: The pledge uses too few legal words.
The pledge arrives after the tempting counting decisions.
The cashier needs a larger bonus.
questions.explanation: The cue is late. It should appear before the count, where rounding and rationalization begin, not after the choices are complete.

questions.prompt: A team wants to reduce small dishonest shortcuts in shared equipment logs without treating every member as a criminal. Which approach best transfers the core move?
choices: Remove all trust and require surveillance for every act.
Rely on private character and avoid any reminders.
Place brief standards directly before the choices where rationalization usually starts.
questions.explanation: The core move is early contextual support for honest self-concept. Total surveillance and no reminders both miss the middle ground where small cheating grows.

reviewCards.front: A small dishonest act still lets someone feel honest. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve self-concept maintenance. People often cheat a little when the act can be rationalized without breaking their honest identity.

reviewCards.front: Where should an honesty cue go?
reviewCards.back: At the front of the act, exactly where the questionable choice begins. A cue after the choice is often too late to interrupt rationalization.

reviewCards.front: Why can a pledge work without extra punishment?
reviewCards.back: It can make the honest self active before the decision. The power is timing and identity, not fear of a new penalty.
When incentives, access, or serious fraud risks overwhelm the gray-edge choice. Reminders support honesty, but they do not replace real controls where stakes are high.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice placing standards before excuses. The skill is finding the exact moment where a small dishonest shortcut begins and moving the reminder there.

ifThenPlans.plan: If someone reconciles money or counts goods, then put the pledge and second initials before the count starts.
If members self-report use, then place the agreement directly above the entry point.
If a report can be softened by loyalty, then print the fairness standard above the line people fill in.
If people claim attendance or credit, then put the attestation before the checklist.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Move one rule, pledge, or standard from an after-the-fact place to the exact spot where the questionable choice begins.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, audit one self-report process and ask where the first rationalization starts. Put a short standard there, not at the end.

memorableLines.text: Put the standard at the front of the act.
memorableLines.why: It makes the timing of honesty cues clear and actionable.

memorableLines.text: The cue did not turn bad people good.
memorableLines.why: It prevents a simplistic character reading of the mechanism.

memorableLines.text: An honesty cue that arrives after the excuse is late to the meeting.
memorableLines.why: It gives timing a memorable, concrete ending.
